::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py svm`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**How do we classify an order as late using a reliable boundary?**

A separating hyperplane gives a linear decision rule; the maximum-margin principle prefers a robust boundary. Primal and dual formulations expose complementary optimisation views, and kernels extend the model to nonlinear feature representations.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
\min_{w,b}\tfrac12\|w\|_2^2\quad\text{s.t. }y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\geq1
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

Our deliberately separable six-order toy labels admit f(d,n)=2d-7. The nearest points lie at distances 3 and 4, with geometric margin 0.5 km under the chosen scaling.

## What to pay attention to

The demonstration shows a valid separator, not a full training optimiser. Real SVMs use regularisation, careful feature scaling, validation and numerical convergence checks.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
